comments.author: @elainepineault2062
comments.text: My paternal grandparents left the island of Fayal in the early 1900s with 6 children and settled in New Bedford, Massachsuetts.. My grandfather was a mason by trade. My dad and 5 more siblings were born in New Bedford. At least one of my grandfather's brothers also settled in New Bedford. My grandmother's sister also accompanied the family to New Bedford.. As a child, I remember letters arriving from friends and family. Cloth bags were sewn and filled with used clothes, the address written right on the cloth and sent to  Fayal. I remember the sadness and concern when the volcano erupted. i may have photos sent to us. For years, a grapevine from a plant my grandfather brought with him grew in our back yard, first its grapebeing made into wine and in later years grape jam. I've never visited but plans are in the work for a family trip back in the near future.

replies.author: @HappyTravel99
replies.text: Thank you so much for sharing this incredibly touching family story. The letters, cloth bags of clothes, your grandfather’s grapevine, and the memories of the volcano all paint such a vivid picture of how deeply Faial remained connected to your family across generations. We hope your family trip becomes a reality soon—you have a beautiful piece of history waiting to be rediscovered. Wishing you an unforgettable journey back to your family’s homeland. ❤

comments.author: @josephrego2527
comments.text:
The beauty of the Azores lives in the hearts of all native Azoreans regardless of where they go. That beauty is so enchanting that it goes on to conquer the hearts and souls of their descendants.  Saudade, the Portuguese word for longing for something close to the heart but can't hold in your arms, is perhaps the best way to describe the relationship. It's impossible for those born there not to love the Azores. Unfortunately, the islands were an economically difficult place to survive. Especially during the late nineteenth and most of the 20th century. So, islanders left in search of a better life elsewhere. Fortunately, since the end of the Estado Novo and Portugal becoming an EU member the economic fortunes of the islands have changed. People still leave but rarely for economic reasons.
These islands are impossible to forget, even if you only visited for a short time.
